Function transformations: grad, vmap and jit

Source: vignettes/transformations.Rmd
transformations.Rmd

A transformation takes an R function and returns a new function. Transformations compose freely: the gradient of a compiled function, a compiled gradient, a vectorized Hessian. This vignette covers all of them.

library(jaxR)

How tracing works

A transformation calls your function with tracers: stand-ins that record the operations applied to them. The function must therefore be written with jaxR operations (jnp_*, lax_*, the R operators) and must be pure: its result depends only on its arguments, and it has no side effects.

make_jaxpr() shows the recorded program.

f <- function(x) jnp_sum(jnp_sin(x) * x)
make_jaxpr(f)(as_jax(c(1, 2, 3)))
#> { lambda ; a:f32[3]. let
#>     b:f32[3] = sin a
#>     c:f32[3] = mul b a
#>     d:f32[] = reduce_sum[axes=0] c
#>   in (d) }

Ordinary R code that does not depend on array values runs once at trace time: loops over a fixed range, if on a shape or on a plain R value, calls to other R functions.

poly <- function(x, coefs) {
  out <- 0
  for (cf in coefs) out <- out * x + cf     # an R loop, unrolled in the trace
  out
}
make_jaxpr(function(x) poly(x, c(1, -2, 3)))(as_jax(2))
#> { lambda ; a:f32[]. let
#>     b:f32[] = mul 0.0 a
#>     c:f32[] = add b 1.0
#>     d:f32[] = mul c a
#>     e:f32[] = add d -2.0
#>     f:f32[] = mul e a
#>     g:f32[] = add f 3.0
#>   in (g) }

R control flow on an array value does not work under tracing, because the tracer has no value. Use jnp_where() or the structured control flow of lax (lax_cond, lax_while_loop, lax_scan; see vignette("lax", package = "jaxR")).

relu_bad <- function(x) if (as.logical(x > 0)) x else 0 * x
tryCatch(grad(relu_bad)(as_jax(1)), error = function(e) class(e)[1])
#> Array f32[] weak_type
#> [1] 1
relu <- function(x) jnp_where(x > 0, x, 0)
grad(relu)(as_jax(1))
#> Array f32[] weak_type
#> [1] 1

Differentiation

grad and value_and_grad

grad(f) returns the gradient of a scalar valued function with respect to its first argument.

x <- as_jax(c(1, 2, 3))
grad(f)(x)
#> Array f32[3]
#> [1]  1.38177323  0.07700372 -2.82885742

argnums selects other arguments (0-based). With several, the result is a list.

loss <- function(w, b, x, y) jnp_mean((x %*% w + b - y)^2)
w <- as_jax(c(0.5, -0.5)); b <- as_jax(0.1)
X <- as_jax(matrix(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6), 3, byrow = TRUE)); y <- as_jax(c(1, 0, 1))
grad(loss)(w, b, X, y)
#> Array f32[2]
#> [1] -6.400000 -8.533334
grad(loss, argnums = c(0L, 1L))(w, b, X, y)
#> [[1]]
#> Array f32[2]
#> [1] -6.400000 -8.533334
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> Array f32[] weak_type
#> [1] -2.133333

Arguments can be nested lists of arrays (pytrees); the gradient has the same structure.

loss2 <- function(params, x, y) jnp_mean((x %*% params$w + params$b - y)^2)
grad(loss2)(list(w = w, b = b), X, y)
#> $w
#> Array f32[2]
#> [1] -6.400000 -8.533334
#> 
#> $b
#> Array f32[] weak_type
#> [1] -2.133333

value_and_grad() returns the value too, and has_aux = TRUE lets the function return extra data that is not differentiated.

value_and_grad(loss)(w, b, X, y)
#> [[1]]
#> Array f32[]
#> [1] 1.36
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> Array f32[2]
#> [1] -6.400000 -8.533334
with_aux <- function(w) {
  r <- X %*% w - y
  list(jnp_mean(r^2), list(residual = r))
}
grad(with_aux, has_aux = TRUE)(w)
#> [[1]]
#> Array f32[2]
#> [1] -7.000000 -9.333334
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [[2]]$residual
#> Array f32[3]
#> [1] -1.5 -0.5 -1.5

Gradients nest, so higher derivatives need nothing new.

g3 <- grad(grad(grad(function(x) x^4)))
g3(as_jax(2))            # 24 x
#> Array f32[] weak_type
#> [1] 48

Forward mode: jvp

jvp(f, primals, tangents) evaluates the function and its directional derivative (Jacobian times vector) in one pass.

jvp(function(x) jnp_sin(x) * x, list(x), list(jnp_ones_like(x)))
#> [[1]]
#> Array f32[3]
#> [1] 0.841471 1.818595 0.423360
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> Array f32[3]
#> [1]  1.38177323  0.07700372 -2.82885742

Reverse mode: vjp

vjp(f, ...) returns the value and a function that maps an output cotangent to the input cotangents (vector times Jacobian).

r <- vjp(function(x) jnp_sin(x) * x, x)
r[[1]]
#> Array f32[3]
#> [1] 0.841471 1.818595 0.423360
r[[2]](as_jax(c(1, 0, 0)))
#> [[1]]
#> Array f32[3]
#> [1] 1.381773 0.000000 0.000000

Two options of vjp() control what is computed and kept. in_nzs marks the inputs that may have a nonzero tangent: the others are treated as constants, and vjp_fun$out_nzs then tells which outputs still depend on a marked input. saveable_args marks the arguments that may be kept for the backward pass. An argument array that the backward pass needs as it is, but that is marked FALSE, is not kept: vjp_fun$args_res shows NotSaveable() in its place, and the caller puts the value back before calling the function (useful when the argument lives elsewhere anyway, so that it is not held twice). Arguments the backward pass does not need show NotNeeded().

a <- as_jax(2, "float32")
b <- as_jax(3, "float32")
r <- vjp(function(x, y) list(x * y, y), a, b, in_nzs = list(TRUE, FALSE))
r[[2]]$out_nzs
#> [[1]]
#> [1] TRUE
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] FALSE
r <- vjp(function(x, y) x * y, a, b, saveable_args = list(TRUE, FALSE))
pullback <- r[[2]]
pullback$args_res
#> [[1]]
#> Array f32[]
#> [1] 2
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> NotSaveable()
pullback$args_res[[2]] <- b
pullback(as_jax(1, "float32"))
#> [[1]]
#> Array f32[]
#> [1] 3
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> Array f32[]
#> [1] 2

linearize

linearize() evaluates once and returns the linear map of the JVP, which can then be applied to many tangents without recomputing the function. linear_transpose() transposes a linear function.

lin <- linearize(function(x) jnp_sin(x) * x, x)
lin[[2]](as_jax(c(1, 0, 0)))
#> Array f32[3]
#> [1] 1.381773 0.000000 0.000000
lt <- linear_transpose(function(v) 3 * v, x)
lt(as_jax(c(1, 1, 1)))
#> [[1]]
#> Array f32[3]
#> [1] 3 3 3

Jacobians and Hessians

jacfwd() builds the Jacobian with forward mode (one pass per input), jacrev() with reverse mode (one pass per output); jacobian() is jacrev(). hessian() is forward over reverse.

g <- function(x) jnp_stack(list(x[0] * x[1], jnp_sin(x[2]), jnp_sum(x^2)))
jacfwd(g)(x)
#> Array f32[3,3]
#>      [,1] [,2]       [,3]
#> [1,]    2    1  0.0000000
#> [2,]    0    0 -0.9899925
#> [3,]    2    4  6.0000000
jacrev(g)(x)
#> Array f32[3,3]
#>      [,1] [,2]       [,3]
#> [1,]    2    1  0.0000000
#> [2,]    0    0 -0.9899925
#> [3,]    2    4  6.0000000
hessian(f)(x)
#> Array f32[3,3]
#>           [,1]      [,2]      [,3]
#> [1,] 0.2391336  0.000000  0.000000
#> [2,] 0.0000000 -2.650888  0.000000
#> [3,] 0.0000000  0.000000 -2.403345

Stopping gradients

stop_gradient() treats a value as a constant.

grad(function(x) jnp_sum(x * stop_gradient(x)))(x)   # only one factor is differentiated
#> Array f32[3]
#> [1] 1 2 3

Integer and boolean inputs

Integers have no tangent space. The cotangent of an integer input has dtype float0, and grad() asks for allow_int = TRUE to differentiate with respect to one.

r <- vjp(function(x, n) x * n, as_jax(c(1, 2)), as_jax(3L))
r[[2]](as_jax(c(1, 1)))
#> [[1]]
#> Array f32[2]
#> [1] 3 3
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> Array float0[] weak_type
#> [1] FALSE

Custom derivatives

custom_jvp() and custom_vjp() replace the derivative of a function, for numerical stability or to differentiate through an iterative solver.

log1pexp <- custom_jvp(
  function(x) jnp_log1p(jnp_exp(x)),
  jvp = function(primals, tangents) {
    x <- primals[[1]]
    list(log1pexp(x), tangents[[1]] * (1 - 1 / (1 + jnp_exp(x))))
  })
grad(log1pexp)(as_jax(100))     # the naive derivative overflows to NaN
#> Array f32[] weak_type
#> [1] 1
grad(function(x) jnp_log1p(jnp_exp(x)))(as_jax(100))
#> Array f32[] weak_type
#> [1] NaN
clip_gradient <- custom_vjp(
  function(x) x,
  fwd = function(x) list(x, NULL),
  bwd = function(res, g) list(jnp_clip(g, -1, 1)))
grad(function(x) jnp_sum(clip_gradient(x) * 10))(x)
#> Array f32[3]
#> [1] 1 1 1

custom_gradient() is the TensorFlow style shortcut and lax_custom_root(), lax_custom_linear_solve() define implicit derivatives of root finders and linear solvers.

Logs and gradient accumulators

A backward rule can send values out of the backward pass. With custom_vjp_defvjp_with_logs() (or custom_gradient(with_logs = TRUE)) the rule returns list(cotangents, logs), where logs is a named list; the with_logs method of a VJP function returns them next to the cotangents, and a plain call drops them. Log names must be unique within one backward pass.

scaled <- custom_gradient(function(x) {
  list(3 * x, function(g) list(3 * g, list(incoming = g)))
}, with_logs = TRUE)
pullback <- vjp(scaled, as_jax(2))[[2]]
pullback$with_logs(as_jax(5))
#> [[1]]
#> [[1]][[1]]
#> Array f32[] weak_type
#> [1] 15
#> 
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [[2]]$incoming
#> Array f32[] weak_type
#> [1] 5
grad(scaled)(as_jax(2))
#> Array f32[] weak_type
#> [1] 3

A rule defined with custom_vjp_defvjp_with_accums() or custom_gradient(with_accums = ) does not return cotangents: it receives one gradient accumulator per argument and pushes contributions into it. A ValAccum sums what acc$accum() receives, a RefAccum exposes a ref, acc$ref, for indexed updates, and an argument that is not differentiated gets a NullAccum, which ignores what it receives. This suits a rule whose cotangent is a sparse update of a large array.

pick <- custom_gradient(function(x, i) {
  list(x[i], function(g, x_acc, i_acc) {
    if (x_acc$kind == "RefAccum") x_acc$ref[i] <- x_acc$ref[i] + g
    NULL
  })
}, with_accums = list(ad_RefAccum, ad_ValAccum))
grad(function(x) pick(x, 2L) * 4)(jnp_arange(5, dtype = "float32"))
#> Array f32[5]
#> [1] 0 0 4 0 0

The with_refs method of a VJP function chooses, per argument, whether the gradient is returned (ad_GradValue()), added into a ref (the ref itself) or not computed (ad_DontWant()); the result holds GradRef() and DidntWant() markers in their places. Inside a backward rule from custom_vjp_defvjp_with_accums(), a leaf can also be an accumulator the rule received, so a nested VJP pushes its gradient straight into it:

sq <- custom_vjp(function(x) x * x)
sq <- custom_vjp_defvjp_with_accums(sq, function(x) list(x * x, x),
  function(r, g, x_acc) {
    vjp(function(x) x * x, r)[[2]]$with_refs(x_acc)(g)
    NULL
  })
grad(sq)(as_jax(3))
#> Array f32[] weak_type
#> [1] 6
pullback <- vjp(function(x, y) x * y, as_jax(3), as_jax(4))[[2]]
acc <- new_ref(as_jax(10, "float32"))
pullback$with_refs(ad_DontWant(), acc)(as_jax(1))
#> [[1]]
#> DidntWant()
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> GradRef()
acc[]
#> Array f32[]
#> [1] 13

Checkpointing

Reverse mode stores the intermediate values of the forward pass. checkpoint() (alias remat()) trades memory for time: the wrapped function is recomputed during the backward pass instead of having its intermediates stored. print_saved_residuals() shows what a function stores.

layer <- function(x) jnp_sin(jnp_sin(x))
deep <- function(x) jnp_sum(checkpoint(layer)(checkpoint(layer)(x)))
grad(deep)(x)
#> Array f32[3]
#> [1]  0.2059352 -0.1366153 -0.9609511

Taylor mode: higher derivatives in one pass

experimental_jet_jet() is the port of jax.experimental.jet. jvp() pushes a value and one tangent through a function; experimental_jet_jet() pushes a value and a whole truncated Taylor series, so the derivatives of order 1 to K along a direction come out of one pass instead of K nested calls of grad() or jvp().

The arguments are the function, the list of its arguments (the point of expansion) and, for each argument, the list of its higher order terms. With the series (1, 0, 0) for a scalar argument the output terms are the first three derivatives:

f <- function(x) jnp_sin(x) * jnp_exp(x)
out <- experimental_jet_jet(f, list(0.4), list(list(1, 0, 0)))
out[[1]]              # f(0.4)
#> Array f32[] weak_type
#> [1] 0.5809439
out[[2]]              # f'(0.4), f''(0.4), f'''(0.4)
#> [[1]]
#> Array f32[] weak_type
#> [1] 1.955005
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> Array f32[] weak_type
#> [1] 2.748123
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> Array f32[] weak_type
#> [1] 1.586235
grad(grad(grad(f)))(0.4)
#> Array f32[] weak_type
#> [1] 1.586235

A series that is not (1, 0, ...) describes a curve through the point, and the result is the Taylor expansion of the function along that curve (Faà di Bruno’s formula). With factorial_scaled = FALSE the terms are Taylor coefficients, the derivatives divided by the factorial of their order. experimental_jet_jet() composes with jit() and vmap(). As in JAX there are rules for arithmetic, the elementary functions, linear structural operations, reductions, products, convolutions and gathers; control flow primitives have none, and custom derivative rules are ignored (the function itself is differentiated).

Vectorization: vmap

vmap(f) maps f over a leading axis of its arguments without a loop: the batch axis is pushed through each primitive.

dot <- function(a, b) jnp_sum(a * b)
A <- as_jax(matrix(1:6, 2, byrow = TRUE), "float32")
B <- as_jax(matrix(6:1, 2, byrow = TRUE), "float32")
vmap(dot)(A, B)
#> Array f32[2]
#> [1] 28 28

in_axes gives the mapped axis of each argument (NULL for an argument that is not mapped) and out_axes places the batch axis of the result.

vmap(dot, in_axes = list(0L, NULL))(A, as_jax(c(1, 1, 1)))
#> Array f32[2]
#> [1]  6 15
vmap(dot, in_axes = list(1L, 1L))(A, B)
#> Array f32[3]
#> [1] 18 20 18
vmap(function(a) a * 2, out_axes = 1L)(A)
#> Array f32[3,2]
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]    2    8
#> [2,]    4   10
#> [3,]    6   12

A common use is per example gradients: differentiate the loss of one example, then map over the batch.

loss1 <- function(w, x, y) (jnp_sum(x * w) - y)^2
vmap(grad(loss1), in_axes = list(NULL, 0L, 0L))(w, X, y)
#> Array f32[3,2]
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]   -3   -6
#> [2,]   -3   -4
#> [3,]  -15  -18

Nested vmap gives all pairs.

vmap(function(a) vmap(function(b) dot(a, b))(B))(A)
#> Array f32[2,2]
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]   28   10
#> [2,]   73   28

axis_name names the mapped axis so that collectives such as lax_psum() can reduce over it from inside the function.

vmap(function(v) v / lax_psum(v, "batch"), axis_name = "batch")(as_jax(c(1, 2, 5)))
#> Array f32[3]
#> [1] 0.125 0.250 0.625

Compilation: jit

jit(f) traces f once per combination of argument shapes and dtypes, compiles the program with XLA and reuses the executable afterwards.

selu <- function(x, alpha = 1.67, lambda = 1.05) lambda * jnp_where(x > 0, x, alpha * jnp_exp(x) - alpha)
selu_jit <- jit(selu)
big <- jnp_linspace(-3, 3, 1000000L)
invisible(selu_jit(big))                 # first call compiles
system.time(for (i in 1:20) block_until_ready(selu(big)))["elapsed"]
#> elapsed 
#>   0.844
system.time(for (i in 1:20) block_until_ready(selu_jit(big)))["elapsed"]
#> elapsed 
#>   0.333

Arguments that decide the structure of the computation (a shape, a flag, a function) must be static: name them in static_argnums or static_argnames. The function is recompiled for each new static value.

make <- jit(function(x, n) jnp_reshape(x, c(n, -1L)), static_argnums = 1L)
make(jnp_arange(6), 2L)
#> Array i32[2,3]
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> [1,]    0    1    2
#> [2,]    3    4    5
make(jnp_arange(6), 3L)
#> Array i32[3,2]
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]    0    1
#> [2,]    2    3
#> [3,]    4    5

A traced value cannot be used where a concrete one is needed; the error says so.

bad <- jit(function(x, n) jnp_reshape(x, c(n, -1L)))
tryCatch(bad(jnp_arange(6), 2L), error = function(e) class(e)[1:2])
#> [1] "jax_type_error" "jax_error"

Useful tools around compilation:

  • disable_jit(code) runs code with jit turned off, to debug with ordinary R tools;
  • log_compiles(code) reports each compilation and explain_cache_misses(code) explains why a function was traced again;
  • clear_caches() drops the compiled executables;
  • eval_shape(f, ...) computes the shapes and dtypes of the result without running f;
  • lower_text(f, ...) returns the StableHLO text of the lowered function;
  • ensure_compile_time_eval(code) evaluates constant operations eagerly during tracing.
eval_shape(function(a, b) a %*% b, ShapeDtypeStruct(c(3L, 4L), "float32"), ShapeDtypeStruct(c(4L, 2L), "float32"))
#> ShapedArray(f32[3,2])
cat(lower_text(function(x) x * 2 + 1, as_jax(c(1, 2))))
#> "builtin.module"() <{sym_name = "jit_fun"}> ({
#>   "func.func"() <{function_type = (tensor<2xf32>) -> tensor<2xf32>, sym_name = "main", sym_visibility = "public"}> ({
#>   ^bb0(%arg0: tensor<2xf32>):
#>     %0 = "stablehlo.constant"() <{value = dense<0x40000000> : tensor<f32>}> : () -> tensor<f32>
#>     %1 = "stablehlo.broadcast_in_dim"(%0) <{broadcast_dimensions = array<i64>}> : (tensor<f32>) -> tensor<2xf32>
#>     %2 = "stablehlo.multiply"(%arg0, %1) : (tensor<2xf32>, tensor<2xf32>) -> tensor<2xf32>
#>     %3 = "stablehlo.constant"() <{value = dense<0x3F800000> : tensor<f32>}> : () -> tensor<f32>
#>     %4 = "stablehlo.broadcast_in_dim"(%3) <{broadcast_dimensions = array<i64>}> : (tensor<f32>) -> tensor<2xf32>
#>     %5 = "stablehlo.add"(%2, %4) : (tensor<2xf32>, tensor<2xf32>) -> tensor<2xf32>
#>     "func.return"(%5) : (tensor<2xf32>) -> ()
#>   }) : () -> ()
#> }) {mhlo.num_partitions = 1 : i32, mhlo.num_replicas = 1 : i32} : () -> ()

Ahead of time compilation, saved executables and the disk cache

jit(f)$lower(...) lowers f for the given arguments (or ShapeDtypeStruct values) and $compile() compiles it; the compiled function only accepts arguments of those shapes and dtypes. As in jax.experimental.serialize_executable, a compiled function can be saved and loaded by a later R session on the same platform with the same XLA runtime, without tracing or compiling again.

compiled <- jit(function(x) jnp_tanh(x) * 2)$lower(as_jax(c(0, 1)))$compile()
s <- experimental_serialize_executable_serialize(compiled)
path <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
saveRDS(s, path)
s <- readRDS(path)
loaded <- experimental_serialize_executable_deserialize_and_load(s[[1]], s[[2]], s[[3]])
loaded(as_jax(c(0.5, 2)))
#> Array f32[2]
#> [1] 0.9242343 1.9280552

The persistent compilation cache does the same automatically: with a cache directory set, every program whose compilation took at least jax_persistent_cache_min_compile_time_secs seconds (default 1) is written there, and later sessions read it back instead of compiling. jax_enable_compilation_cache = FALSE turns it off. A cached file is native code, so use a directory only you can write to.

experimental_compilation_cache_set_cache_dir(file.path(tempdir(), "jax_cache"))
jax_config_update("jax_persistent_cache_min_compile_time_secs", 0)
invisible(jit(function(x) jnp_cos(x) + 1)(as_jax(1)))
length(list.files(file.path(tempdir(), "jax_cache"))) > 0
#> [1] TRUE
jax_config_update("jax_compilation_cache_dir", NULL)
jax_config_update("jax_persistent_cache_min_compile_time_secs", 1)

Composition

The transformations are designed to be combined in any order.

per_example_hessian <- jit(vmap(hessian(function(x) jnp_sum(x^3))))
per_example_hessian(as_jax(matrix(c(1, 2, 3, 4), 2)))
#> Array f32[2,2,2]
#> [0, , ]
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]    6    0
#> [2,]    0   18
#> [1, , ]
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]   12    0
#> [2,]    0   24

Summary of the transformation API

Function Purpose
grad, value_and_grad gradient of a scalar function
jvp, linearize forward mode
vjp, linear_transpose reverse mode
jacfwd, jacrev, jacobian, hessian full derivative matrices
stop_gradient block differentiation
custom_jvp, custom_vjp, custom_gradient user defined derivative rules
checkpoint (remat), checkpoint_policies, print_saved_residuals memory and time trade-off in reverse mode
experimental_jet_jet Taylor mode: derivatives of order 1 to K in one pass
fwd_and_bwd, closure_convert, linear_call lower level building blocks
vmap, sequential_vmap, custom_vmap vectorization and user defined batching rules
jit, disable_jit, clear_caches, make_jaxpr, eval_shape, lower_text compilation and inspection
experimental_serialize_executable_serialize, experimental_compilation_cache_set_cache_dir saved executables and the disk cache
named_call, named_scope names in the lowered program
